query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, the onset and progression of premelting are governed by local composition fluctuations at surfaces and grain boundaries that reduce the local melting temperature, initiating a multi-step melting transition from these interfacial regions inward.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-state FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, synthesized as a nominally single-phase mixture.
generation.intervention: Subject nanoparticles to rapid in situ heating in a transmission electron microscope (TEM) from ambient up to near the alloy’s bulk melting range, with time-resolved electron diffraction and elemental mapping to capture changes in structure and composition in real time.
generation.conditions: Heating under high vacuum or inert gas to temperatures spanning from below to above the known bulk solidus (up to ~1600 K), using size-selected nanoparticles (~5–50 nm).
generation.structural_mediator: Depletion or enrichment of certain constituents at surfaces/grain boundaries, altering local free energies and enabling partial melt formation at lower temperatures than the nominal bulk.
generation.mechanism: Thermally driven surface and grain boundary diffusion leads to localized enrichment of lower-melting components, lowering the effective local melting point and causing partial liquid formation that expands inward with increasing temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Electron diffraction patterns will exhibit early-onset diffraction peak broadening or splitting near surfaces, followed by progressive, localized emergence of liquid-like scattering, leading to complete melting within the particles at temperatures below or spanning the nominal bulk melting point.
generation.baseline: Under slower heating rates or more compositionally uniform nanoparticles, melting should proceed more uniformly at a temperature closer to the bulk solidus.
generation.boundary: May become invalid for extremely large or ultrafine nanoparticles, or in conditions that eliminate compositional gradients (e.g., very slow heating allowing equilibrium, or very fast quenches that freeze transient states).
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature offsets for initial melt formation cannot be precisely predicted from existing data and may depend strongly on size distributions, heating rate, and local stoichiometry.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare two sets of identically sized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with different degrees of compositional homogeneity and observe melting via in situ high-speed TEM heating. Track diffraction peak evolution and the spatial initiation of melting in each sample.
measurements: Time-stamped electron diffraction patterns to detect peak shifts, broadening, and the emergence of diffuse scattering.
Elemental mapping of surfaces and core to identify composition gradients.
High-resolution TEM imaging of nanoparticle surface/center before, during, and after heating.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If melting occurs uniformly in the nanoparticle volume at a single temperature, with no evidence of localized or early onset melting at surfaces or boundaries, this would contradict the hypothesis.

In 2018, a carbothermal shock method was reported by Yao et al. to alloy up to eight elements into HEA NPs with the designated composition and size. This method involves a 55-ms heating of mixed metal precursors on carbon supports at a peak temperature of 2000 K in argon and cooling at a cooling rate of ∼105 K/s. The high temperature ensures uniform mixtures of multiple elements by fission/fusion and catalytically driven particle dispersion mechanisms. This work has made an important step in the rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. However, this method can only be applied to conductive, surface-oxidized carbon support materials. The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. However, the common extreme high temperature related approaches such as arc melting and laser cladding are not suitable for supporting HEA-NPs due to the rapid growth and aggregation of nanoparticles. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM. decision.trend: Early work on 3d transition-element high-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) established how elevated temperatures affect phase stability and magnetic/spin states (PMC6093928). Subsequent in situ approaches visualized the formation and high-temperature dynamics of multi-element metallic nanoparticles, implicating microstructural transitions and support interactions in determining thermal stability (PMC7733500). Later studies demonstrated scalable high-entropy nanoparticle synthesis methods using high-enthalpy routes (plasma jets, laser irradiation), but left open questions on the precise onset and progression of premelting (PMC10873330, PMC11427457). While these efforts revealed new processing pathways and some thermodynamic drivers, they did not fully resolve how phase transition mechanisms unfold under near-melting conditions in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy nanoparticles.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in characterizing and synthesizing high-entropy nanoparticles at elevated temperatures, the micro-to-nanoscale mechanisms that trigger premelting and govern how partial melts evolve remain elusive for FeNiCrCoCu systems. The interplay between local compositional fluctuations, surface diffusion, and dynamic atomic rearrangements has not been mapped in real time, leaving the precise onset conditions and controlling processes insufficiently understood.
decision.lever: High-speed in situ TEM heating of size-selected FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, coupled with time-resolved electron diffraction and elemental mapping
decision.why: Building on prior demonstrations of in situ high-temperature nanoparticle formation and stability (PMC7733500) and rapid synthesis (PMC10873330, PMC11427457), a dedicated in situ heating experiment focusing on FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles would directly visualize atomic diffusion pathways and surface changes as temperature approaches the melting point. Time-resolved imaging and diffraction can thus pinpoint the onset temperature of premelting and track how the transition progresses. This approach follows logically from the trend of in situ studies aiming to elucidate real-time structural and compositional changes under extreme thermal conditions.
